extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in copyright law, plagiarism disputes, and Canadian case law
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the Deeks v Wells (1932) litigation about alleged plagiarism/copyright infringement and related breach-of-trust claims, including trial, appellate, and Privy Council reasoning and legacy. Useful as a case-summary and source of the evidentiary and legal standards applied in such disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of access to plaintiff's manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimant must show that the defendant had access to the plaintiff's manuscript or work (e.g., that Macmillan of Canada sent the manuscript to Britain or that Wells had seen it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct evidence of access (custodial testimony, documentary proof of transmission) is highly persuasive; absence of direct evidence undermined Deeks' claim. Courts gave weight to testimony denying access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity alone is insufficient to prove copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities in outline, approach, terms, or organization between two histories do not by themselves establish copyright infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the courts held, 'histories on similar topics will use similar terms and organization' and common topical overlap or common sources can explain resemblance; plaintiffs must show more than general similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and specificity of expert comparative textual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert witnesses who perform textual comparisons must present cogent, significant, and specific correspondences, not general or speculative assertions of similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial court rejected Professor Irwin's memorandum as 'just solemn nonsense' and 'not reasons at all.' Expert comparisons should identify probative, non‑generic correspondences that cannot be explained by common sources or coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and weight of witness testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges evaluate the credibility of defendant, publisher, and expert witnesses; credible denials by defendants/publishers can be decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Deeks, the courts accepted Wells' and Macmillan representatives' testimony over the plaintiff's experts. Credibility determinations can dispose of cases where direct testimony contradicts circumstantial inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain of custody and manuscript handling evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence about who had possession of the manuscript and how it was handled (e.g., testimony that the manuscript 'had always been in [Saul's] possession') is material to proving whether the work was transmitted to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary or witness evidence showing the manuscript never left a particular custodian undermines an access allegation and supports a defence against copying claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility/timing of independent creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that it was physically possible for the defendant to have prepared the accused work in the time available bears on whether independent creation is plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts may reject claims that independent authorship was impossible unless timing evidence convincingly establishes impossibility; in Deeks, the court held Wells could have written The Outline in the time he had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by common sources or shared authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When both works rely on the same sources or reference material, similarities may be attributable to common sources rather than copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether alleged parallels are the predictable result of drawing on identical source material; if so, they are not probative of plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of circumstantial evidence to rebut direct evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstantial comparative evidence must be strong enough to rebut direct testimony or documentary evidence that negates access or copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Atkin and lower courts required the comparative evidence to be sufficient to overcome direct evidence that the manuscript never left Canada; weak circumstantial comparisons were inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required for breach of trust by intermediary (publisher)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a breach of trust by a publisher or intermediary, the plaintiff must prove improper disclosure or misuse of the manuscript by that intermediary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denials by publisher representatives and evidence of internal handling procedures (e.g., board review processes) can defeat breach-of-trust claims unless contradicted by reliable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate deference to factual findings on evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher courts (including the Judicial Committee) generally do not re‑hear pure evidential/factual disputes and will defer to lower courts' findings unless there is a compelling reason to revisit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Privy Council noted it normally does not re‑hear evidential issues but may do so in exceptional circumstances (e.g., a litigant appearing in person and forcefully pursuing points), though it still gave deference to the factual conclusions below in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation risk and costs when claim lacks sufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs pursuing weak or insufficiently supported claims risk dismissal and an order to pay defendants' court costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Deeks, the action was dismissed and Deeks was ordered to pay costs; litigants should weigh the evidentiary strength of their case before pursuing high‑value claims.
